lessons.title: Building Reliable ML Data Pipelines
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Most model failures are data failures

A model rarely fails because the architecture was wrong. It fails because a column silently changed type, a join leaked the future, or a backfill ran twice and duplicated half the training set. ML engineering starts with treating data movement as production software: versioned, tested, idempotent, and observable.

## Pipeline principles that actually matter

1. **Reproducibility.** Given the same commit and the same inputs, you must be able to rebuild the same dataset. That means versioning data (DVC, LakeFS, or Delta Lake time travel) and pinning transform code.
2. **Idempotency.** Re-running a pipeline step must not corrupt state. Write to partitions atomically and use upserts keyed on stable IDs instead of blind appends.
3. **Schema enforcement.** Validate at ingestion: expected columns, types, nullability, value ranges. A schema check that fails loudly beats a model that fails silently three weeks later.
4. **Validation over hope.** Tools like Great Expectations, Soda, or Pandera let you assert statistical properties — no nulls in user_id, event timestamps within the last 7 days, label distribution within tolerance.

## Orchestration: Airflow, Dagster, Prefect

Airflow remains the workhorse: mature, huge operator ecosystem, but DAG-centric thinking fits ETL better than ML. Dagster's asset-centric model maps naturally to datasets and models as versioned assets with lineage. Prefect sits between, with a lighter developer experience. Pick one and standardize; the worst pipeline is three orchestrators duct-taped together.

```python
import dagster as dg
import pandera as pa
from pandera.typing import Series

class EventsSchema(pa.DataFrameModel):
    user_id: Series[int] = pa.Field(nullable=False)
    event_ts: Series[pa.DateTime] = pa.Field(nullable=False)
    amount: Series[float] = pa.Field(ge=0)

@dg.asset
def validated_events(raw_events) -> dg.Output:
    df = EventsSchema.validate(raw_events)
    return dg.Output(df, metadata={'rows': len(df)})
```

## Batch vs streaming

Batch (Spark, dbt on a warehouse) is simpler, cheaper, and sufficient for daily-retrained models. Streaming (Kafka + Flink or Spark Structured Streaming) buys freshness at the cost of operational complexity — exactly-once semantics, late data, state backends. Default to batch until a product requirement forces sub-hour freshness.

## Lineage and observability

Every pipeline needs a paper trail: which code version produced which dataset, and which dataset trained which model. Lineage tools (OpenLineage/Marquez, or Dagster's built-in asset lineage) answer the question 'which upstream change broke this model?' in minutes instead of days. Emit structured metrics from every stage — rows in, rows out, null rates, runtime — and alert on anomalies, not just failures. A pipeline that silently drops 30% of rows is worse than one that crashes; crashes get fixed.

## Exercise

Sketch the pipeline for one model you own or want to build: list each stage, mark where data is versioned, and add one validation check per stage. If you cannot name the check, that stage is where your next incident comes from.

lessons.title: Feature Stores: Killing Training-Serving Skew
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## The skew problem

Training-serving skew is the silent killer of model performance: features computed one way offline and a slightly different way online. A classic example — a 7-day rolling average computed over event time in training but over processing time in serving. Your offline metrics look great; production degrades, and nothing in the model changed.

## What a feature store gives you

A feature store separates feature definition from execution. You declare features once (a FeatureView in Feast), and the store guarantees the same transformation logic feeds both the offline store (for training) and the online store (for low-latency serving). The critical mechanism is point-in-time correctness: when building a training set, each row gets feature values as they were known at that timestamp — no future leakage.

```python
from feast import FeatureView, Field, FileSource
from feast.types import Float32, Int64
from datetime import timedelta

orders_source = FileSource(path='data/orders.parquet', timestamp_field='event_ts')

user_features = FeatureView(
    name='user_order_features',
    entities=['user'],
    ttl=timedelta(days=30),
    schema=[Field(name='avg_order_value_7d', dtype=Float32),
            Field(name='order_count_7d', dtype=Int64)],
    source=orders_source,
)
```

Materialize to the online store (Redis, DynamoDB) for serving; query historical features for training through a single API.

## Trade-offs

Managed platforms (Tecton) buy you on-call-free operations and streaming support at real cost. Open-source Feast is flexible and cheap but you own the infrastructure. Freshness costs money: real-time features need streaming pipelines and online stores — ask whether the business actually needs 50ms-fresh features or whether hourly batch is fine. Backfills are the operational tax; budget for them.

## Point-in-time joins in practice

The mechanism that makes feature stores worth it is the point-in-time join. At training time you hand the store an entity dataframe — say, (user_id, event_timestamp) pairs for every historical prediction you want to simulate — and it returns feature values computed only from data available at each timestamp. Two operational details bite practitioners: first, your TTL must cover your longest feature window, or old training rows silently get nulls; second, late-arriving data needs a defined policy — either accept approximate features for recent rows or delay materialization. Test consistency directly: sample production requests, recompute their features offline, and diff. If the numbers disagree, your serving path has diverged from your training path and no amount of model tuning will save you.

## Exercise

Pick three features for a model you care about. For each, write the entity, the aggregation window, and the serving latency budget. Then decide: batch-computed or streaming? Defend the choice in one sentence each.

lessons.title: Distributed Training and Experiment Tracking
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## When one GPU is not enough

Models and datasets outgrow single GPUs. Your options, in order of complexity: gradient accumulation (simulate large batches for free), data-parallel training with DDP (each GPU holds a full model replica, gradients averaged), FSDP or DeepSpeed ZeRO (shard model parameters and optimizer states across GPUs to fit bigger models), and finally pipeline or tensor parallelism for the largest models. Most practitioners never need more than DDP plus ZeRO-2 or ZeRO-3.

```bash
torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 train.py --deepspeed ds_config.json
```

Memory math matters: Adam keeps two optimizer states per parameter in fp32, so plan for roughly 4x the parameter count in bytes for fp16 training with Adam before activations are counted. Gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory; mixed precision (fp16/bf16) roughly halves most of it.

## Track everything or it did not happen

An experiment tracker is your lab notebook. MLflow is the pragmatic default: open source, self-hostable, with a model registry built in. Weights & Biases is the polished SaaS option with better visualizations and collaboration. Log hyperparameters, code version, data version, metrics per step, and artifacts (checkpoints, plots). The rule: any run you cannot reproduce from its logged metadata is a rumor, not an experiment.

```python
import mlflow
with mlflow.start_run():
    mlflow.log_params({'lr': 3e-5, 'batch_size': 128, 'epochs': 3})
    mlflow.log_metric('val_loss', 0.412, step=1000)
    mlflow.pytorch.log_model(model, 'model')
```

## Trade-offs

Spot or preemptible instances cut GPU bills 60-80% but demand checkpointing and restart-tolerant code. Reproducibility costs discipline: seed everything, lock environments (Docker plus lockfiles), and log the data version — a fixed seed means nothing if the data changed.

## Debugging distributed runs

Distributed training fails in ways single-GPU training never does. The classic is the silent hang: one rank crashes or stalls on data loading and the rest wait forever at a collective operation. Defenses: always prototype on one GPU first, use torchrun's elastic rendezvous so failed nodes can rejoin, and set NCCL timeouts aggressively in development so hangs surface as errors. Log per-rank throughput — a rank at half speed usually means a straggler disk or bad NUMA affinity. For spot instances, checkpoint every N steps to durable storage (not local disk) and make your script resume-aware: on restart it should discover the latest checkpoint and continue, not start over. Test the resume path deliberately by killing a run mid-training; the first time you test it should not be during a real preemption.

## Exercise

Take your last training run. Write down everything you would need to reproduce it exactly. Whatever is missing (data version? seed? environment?) is your tracking gap — close one gap this week.

lessons.title: Deploying Models: Batch, Online, and Streaming Inference
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Choose the serving pattern first

Batch scoring (nightly jobs scoring millions of rows) is cheapest and simplest — a scheduled Spark or Python job writing predictions to a table. Online serving (REST/gRPC, milliseconds) serves live traffic and needs autoscaling, health checks, and strict latency SLOs. Streaming (Kafka/Flink scoring events as they arrive) fits fraud and personalization. Match the pattern to the product's latency requirement, not to hype.

## The serving stack

Triton Inference Server is the production workhorse: model versioning, dynamic batching, concurrent model execution, and backends for PyTorch, TensorRT, and ONNX. For simpler services, BentoML or Ray Serve wrap a model in an API with Docker packaging and autoscaling. KServe adds serverless scale-to-zero on Kubernetes. For LLMs specifically, vLLM (PagedAttention, continuous batching) is the default high-throughput choice.

```python
import bentoml
from bentoml.io import NumpyNdarray

runner = bentoml.pytorch.get('fraud_model:latest').to_runner()

svc = bentoml.Service('fraud_svc', runners=[runner])

@svc.api(input=NumpyNdarray(), output=NumpyNdarray())
async def predict(features):
    return await runner.predict.async_run(features)
```

## Optimize for your SLO

Quantization (INT8 via ONNX Runtime or TensorRT) can cut latency 2-4x with small accuracy cost — measure, do not assume. Dynamic batching trades a few milliseconds of latency for big throughput gains. Autoscale on GPU utilization or queue depth (KEDA), not just CPU. And always load-test with realistic payloads before launch; a model that passes unit tests can still OOM under concurrent requests.

## Trade-offs

Managed endpoints (SageMaker, Vertex AI) trade cost for zero ops burden. Self-hosting on Kubernetes trades ops burden for control and cost. GPUs idle expensively — scale-to-zero or batch where you can.

## Capacity planning without guesswork

Size serving capacity from measured numbers, not vibes. Benchmark one replica: max sustainable requests per second at your p99 latency target, and GPU memory at that concurrency. Then capacity = peak traffic / per-replica throughput, plus 20-30% headroom for deploys and spikes. Two knobs move the math most: batching — dynamic batching on Triton or vLLM's continuous batching can multiply throughput 3-10x for a few ms of added latency — and precision, where INT8 or FP8 halves memory and roughly doubles throughput on supported hardware. Watch the failure mode nobody load-tests: cold starts. A 13B model can take minutes to load onto a GPU; if your autoscaler reacts to a spike by adding replicas that take 3 minutes to warm, you need over-provisioning or pre-warmed pools, not just reactive scaling.

## Exercise

Define an SLO for one model: p99 latency, throughput, and availability. Then pick the serving pattern and one optimization from this lesson, and write the one paragraph you would put in a design doc defending the choice.

lessons.title: Monitoring, Drift Detection, and CI/CD for ML
lessons.contentMarkdown:
## Models rot

Deployed models decay: data drift (input distributions shift — PSI or KS tests catch this), concept drift (the relationship between inputs and labels changes — only labeled feedback catches this), and plain pipeline breakage. Monitor three layers: infrastructure (latency, error rate, throughput via Prometheus and Grafana), data (feature distributions, missing rates, schema violations via Evidently or WhyLabs), and outcomes (business metrics, prediction distributions, and — where labels arrive late — proxy metrics).

## The model registry as source of truth

Every promoted model gets a versioned entry: training data hash, code commit, metrics, and approval state. MLflow's registry (Staging to Production to Archived) or a similar flow makes rollbacks boring, which is the goal. Champion/challenger setups route a slice of traffic to the new model so you compare on live data before full cutover.

## CI/CD for ML

ML CI/CD differs from software CI/CD: the build is training, and it is expensive and nondeterministic. A sane pipeline: data change or schedule triggers retraining, then automated data tests and a baseline model-quality gate (must beat the champion on a held-out set), then shadow or canary deployment, then automated rollback if live metrics degrade. Keep training code, inference code, and feature code in one repo so a change to any of them runs the same tests.

## Trade-offs

Retraining frequency is a cost/benefit call: daily retraining on stable data is mostly GPU-burning theater. Canary deployments need enough traffic for statistical significance — low-traffic models may be better served by shadow scoring and offline evaluation.

## Alert on symptoms, dashboard the rest

The fastest way to burn out an ML on-call rotation is alerting on every drift metric. Alert only on things that demand a human now: serving error rate above SLO, p99 latency breach, prediction volume collapsing to zero, or schema violations blocking the pipeline. Everything else — PSI drift scores, feature null rates, calibration curves — belongs on dashboards reviewed on a cadence (daily for high-stakes models, weekly otherwise). For drift specifically, set thresholds from history: alert when the drift score exceeds the 99th percentile of its last 30 days, not on an arbitrary 0.2 cutoff that pages you every Monday. And every alert needs a runbook link: what to check, how to roll back, who owns the model. An alert without a runbook is just anxiety with a pager.

## Exercise checklist

Build this checklist for your next deployment: data validation tests pass; model beats champion on holdout; canary or shadow plan defined; rollback runbook written; drift alerts configured; owner on call named. Ship only when every box is checked.
